title: Game Twelve, Second Half
part: PART FOUR: THE OTHER KIND OF CONFIDENCE

pages.text:
*Way to Lose #51: Miss the last shot.*

The second half kicks off with a thud, a hard, ugly sound that vibrates right through the turf. Northgate’s striker fires from close range. It isn’t a great shot, but Priya has already saved three in the last two minutes, and her arms feel like they are made of wet clay. The ball slips through her gloves and into the net. Two to one.

The noise from the Northgate crowd rises like a sudden, sharp spike. Priya does not look at the net. Instead, she stares at the dirt under her cleats, her shoulders hunched so low she looks like she is trying to disappear into the grass.

I jog back to her. I do not say "It's okay." I do not say "Shake it off." I stop right in front of her and tap her oversized gloves, just once.

"Angles," I say.

It is the code we practiced, the one true thing she knows regardless of the score. Priya looks up. Her eyes are wide and wet behind her sports band. She takes a deep breath, her chest expanding, and straightens her spine.

Then the next shot comes, a rocket from the left wing. Priya is there. She does not flinch. She tracks the ball, reads the line, and moves to the spot before the ball arrives. She tips it over the bar.

The bench stands up. Ollie drops an orange slice. No one notices.
pages.image: A tiny girl in oversized goalkeeper gloves stands in front of a soccer net, looking up calmly; a wiry girl with a yellow armband stands nearby tapping the goalkeeper's glove; a muddy field and a duck pond are visible in the background.

pages.text:
We push, driving forward with our shoulders and our lungs.

Josie is on the wing, and she is talking. She always talks, but this time it is different. This is not panic. This is a play-by-play.

"Ruiz has the ball," she shouts, her voice cutting through the wind. "She is looking left. She is looking right. She is looking for a pass."

I hear myself in her voice. For months, that voice in my head has been a sarcastic announcer, mocking every mistake and highlighting every flaw. But right now, as I control the ball and see the space open up, the description is just a description.

There is no sarcasm. There is no judgment. There is only the fact that I am here, and the ball is moving.

Ahmed is tracking back. He is actually tracking back. I see him check his shoulder, see me, and wait. He does not run. He holds his position. He is trusting me.

The ball sits at my feet. It is heavy, but it is mine. I pass it to Josie. She takes it one touch and cuts inside. The Northgate defender slides. Josie steps over the legs. She is flying.

The crowd gasps. It is a single, held breath.

I am not watching the scoreboard. I am watching Josie. I am watching the game. And for the first time, the game is enough.
pages.image: A girl with wild curly hair dribbles a soccer ball past a sliding opponent on a muddy field; a wiry girl in a yellow armband watches intently from the midfield; the background is blurred with motion.

pages.text:
Minute forty-seven.

Josie reaches the edge of the box and, instead of shooting, she whips a cross into the air. The ball hangs there, spinning slowly against the gray sky.

Ollie is waiting for it. He has spent the whole game on the bench with his orange slices, but now he is in the box, eyes fixed upward. He isn't the tallest or the fastest, but he jumps exactly where the ball is going. His head connects with the leather, dropping it soft and sweet right to Ahmed’s feet.

Ahmed looks at the goal. He has the speed to score the winner. He could end this right now.

Then he looks at me.

I am three yards away, in a better position, wearing the yellow armband. Ahmed smiles, a small, quick thing.

"Yours," he says.

He taps it back to me.

I don't think or calculate. I just swing. My leg comes around, clean and strong, and the ball hits the net.

Two to two.

The park does something I can't describe. It is not a cheer. It is a release, like the moment the last bell rings on a test you actually passed.

Kai Brandt, the Northgate striker, stops running. He claps his hands slowly. He looks at me, and he nods.

I want to cry. I want to scream. I want to run to the bench and hug Ollie. But I stay still. I breathe.
pages.image: A lanky boy hands a soccer ball to a wiry girl with a yellow armband in a soccer box; a small boy with orange slices in a bag watches from the sideline; the goal net is visible behind them.

pages.text:
Minute forty-nine. The final two minutes stretch out, and my heart beats like a drum solo I cannot stop. Northgate kicks a long ball down the left side, that slanted stretch where we have never defended well, but this time Tank is waiting for it. Leo and Mateo stand right beside him, the three of them forming a wall that actually stays put.

The ball goes out for a throw-in. The crowd gets loud, and the Northgate coach is yelling, his hands wild as he draws diagrams in the air again. Then comes the corner kick. The ball flies in ugly, bouncing off the ground, then a shin, then a knee until it drops into Kai's feet.

He strikes it. Three to two. The noise becomes a physical weight pressing against my ears, the vibration humming right through my chest. There is time for one more kick, the clock still reading forty-nine.

The ball is cleared to midfield and comes to me, thirty yards out. I look at the goal, then at Priya, who stands tall and watches the ball with steady eyes. I take it up the middle, deciding not to curve it or aim for the corner, but straight for the center.

I strike it. It is the cleanest shot I have ever hit, my leg snapping like a whip, the ball flying true. It hits the crossbar. *Clack.*

The whistle blows. The ball bounces off the bar and lands in the grass. The game is over.
pages.image: A soccer ball hits the top of a goal crossbar and bounces away; a wiry girl with a yellow armband stands frozen with her hands on her head; a crowd of players stands in the background.

pages.text:
I stand there, hands on my head, exactly where I stood after the own goal. I wait for the heavy feeling of worthlessness to sweep me off my feet, expecting to turn into nothing. It does not come.

The minutes stretch out while the other teams walk off, and I find Priya. She is not looking at the ground, but at me, and she gives me a small thumbs up. Over by the bench, Tank is hugging the twins. Leo and Mateo are in his arms, and for the first time all season, they are not arguing. They are just being held.

Josie is quiet. She is looking at her cleats, breathing hard, not talking. Coach Gin walks to the sideline, ignoring the scoreboard to look directly at me.

"Information," she says.

Just that word.

I laugh, and it starts in my chest, coming out as a happy sob that hurts my ribs. I laugh until I am crying.

That night, in my room, I open the red notebook.

Way to Lose #51: Miss the last shot.

I look at the line, then at the loss. Underneath, in my own handwriting, I write: Also: the best game we've ever played.
